subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Time Dilation Near Black Holes
description: A 60-second lesson on Time Dilation Near Black Holes.

hook.text: Near a black hole, time slows down. A clock near the event horizon ticks slower than one far away.

buildup.text: Einstein's general relativity predicts this: stronger gravity means slower time. It's called gravitational time dilation.

discovery.text: GPS satellites must correct for time dilation caused by Earth's gravity. Near a black hole, the effect is extreme.

twist.text: Spending an hour near a black hole could mean years pass for everyone else—exactly as shown in the film Interstellar.

climax.text: At the event horizon, time stops from an outside observer's view. The falling person sees everything continue normally.

punchline.text: Time bends near black holes. One person's hour is another's century.

quiz.question: What happens to time near a black hole's event horizon?
options: Time slows dramatically compared to a distant observer
Time speeds up due to the intense energy
Time reverses direction inside the event horizon

details.summary: General relativity predicts that time slows down in strong gravitational fields. Near a black hole's event horizon, time passes dramatically slower relative to distant observers.
details.whyItMatters: Gravitational time dilation is one of general relativity's most counterintuitive predictions, confirmed by precision experiments. Near black holes, it reaches extreme levels that fundamentally alter our understanding of time.
takeaways: Time slows dramatically near a black hole's event horizon
A falling object appears frozen in time to distant observers
The effect is the extreme version of gravitational time dilation

faq.question: Is the time dilation in the movie Interstellar realistic?
faq.answer: The premise is scientifically grounded. Near a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole, extreme time dilation is possible — one hour could equal years elsewhere. Physicist Kip Thorne consulted on the film. The specific ratios depicted required a black hole spinning at 99.99% of maximum.

faq.question: Does GPS rely on gravitational time dilation corrections?
faq.answer: Yes. GPS satellites experience weaker gravity than ground clocks, making them tick faster by about 45 microseconds per day. Without relativistic corrections, GPS positions would drift by roughly 10 km daily. This is gravitational time dilation in everyday technology.
